analysis.one_liner: Extends consumer financial protections for servicemembers under Consumer Financial Protection Bureau oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2017 with 16 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Banking Committee, which took no action before Congress ended, so it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau the power to enforce a set of existing servicemember protections — limits on interest rates on debts taken on before military service, eviction safeguards, caps on lease terms for cars, break rights for phone contracts, and rules against default judgments while serving. Right now those rules exist in the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, but the CFPB's enforcement authority over them is limited. The bill would close that gap by adding those sections of the law to the list of statutes the CFPB can police [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers, reservists called to duty, and their families, who would gain a federal consumer regulator able to act when lenders, landlords, auto dealers, and phone carriers take advantage of them during deployments [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds key sections of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act — covering interest rate caps on pre-service debts, default judgments, evictions, mortgages, motor vehicle leases, telephone service contracts, and installment purchase contracts — to the statutes the CFPB can enforce [S2] [S3].
Extends coverage to reservists ordered to report for military service and persons ordered to report for induction, closing a gap in who is protected during mobilization [S2].
Excludes only narrow areas — insurance, bailments, and child custody proceedings — so the enforcement power would reach the financial contracts servicemembers most commonly deal with [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders, auto dealers and finance companies, mortgage servicers, debt collectors, and wireless carriers, who would face a federal regulator with authority to investigate and penalize violations against military borrowers [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Criminating-style enforcement by a single federal bureau could impose penalties on businesses for conduct that state courts already police through the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act itself, raising duplication questions [S3].
The bill leaves out insurance and child custody matters from CFPB authority, so some disputes servicemembers face would remain outside the bureau's reach [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted but real: military families facing deployments are a classic group that predatory lenders and repossession-heavy auto lenders single out, and giving an existing regulator clear authority is a low-cost fix. The cost falls on firms that profit from servicemembers' difficulty defending themselves in court while deployed, which is exactly the conduct the underlying law already declares illegal. Honest supporters would acknowledge the bill adds enforcement on top of existing private rights of action rather than creating new substantive protections.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took the bill up after referral, and it died there when this Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on June 21, 2017 with 15 Democratic cosponsors signed onto the original text, for 16 total Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced; that is the last action in the record [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders, auto finance companies, debt collectors, and wireless carriers that profit from servicemembers' contracts are better off, since the CFPB never gained enforcement authority over these military protections. Servicemembers and their families gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Military Consumer Enforcement Act to extend CFPB enforcement to servicemember financial protections.

for.name: 16 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Brown, Warren, Duckworth,Tester, Blumenthal, Kaine, Baldwin, Klobuchar, Menendez, Durbin and others

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-controlled Banking Committee never took the bill up [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Consumer lenders, payday and installment lenders, and debt collectors
industries.note: These firms would face CFPB investigations and penalties for lending that violates servicemember protections, including the 6% interest cap on pre-service debts. Their business often depends on borrowers who cannot easily fight back while deployed.

industries.industry: Auto dealers and auto finance companies
industries.note: Motor vehicle leases and installment purchase contracts are covered, so repossession and lease-termination practices against servicemembers would come under federal enforcement. Servicemembers have historically been targets of auto lending abuses.

Telephone service contracts are covered, meaning carriers could no longer enforce early-termination and contract terms against servicemembers who get orders to move or deploy without facing a federal regulator.
Mortgages, deeds of trust, and eviction protections are covered, so foreclosures and evictions of deployed servicemembers would face CFPB enforcement on top of existing court remedies.
